root.note: Wiktionary takes it back to an Indo-European word for water, reconstructed as *h₂ekʷeh₂.

history: Eau is three letters for one sound, /o/, and each letter is a fossil. It is Latin aqua, worn down over a thousand years of speech. The oldest French text that has it, the Life of Saint Alexis from around 1050, writes egua. The Song of Roland, around 1100, has ewe, and a text of 1185 writes eaue. The modern spelling eau is attested from 1490. The sounds kept shrinking, but the spelling stayed behind, which is why French writes eau and says o. The plural eaux is said the same way. Remember the gender as well: eau is feminine, so it is l'eau froide, ‘cold water’, and une eau minérale.
historyEinfach: Eau comes from the Latin word aqua. In old French texts it was written egua, ewe and eaue. The sounds became shorter and shorter, but the spelling did not change so much. That is why you write eau but say only o. Eau is feminine: l'eau froide.
